claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is a single-phase solid solution with a uniform distribution of constituent elements.
High mechanical loading causes plastic strain to localize at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary strain localization triggers local phase instability or precipitation of brittle secondary phases.
The load-induced grain-boundary phases compromise dislocation transfer and energy dissipation.
Compromised dislocation transfer and energy dissipation lead to loss of toughness and brittle fracture.
The controlled comparison uses an as-cast single-phase group and a mildly thermally treated group that has not fully recrystallized.
Testing should use graded high-strain-rate tensile or compressive loading.
At high stress, grain-boundary localization can overwhelm dislocation-mediated plasticity in the bulk.
Grain boundaries under load act as nucleation sites for brittle secondary phases.
Brittle intergranular regions reduce distributed deformation and promote crack initiation and propagation.
Samples that lose toughness will exhibit nanoscale precipitates or local compositional segregation at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary phase instability will correlate with reduced ductility, toughness, and total strain before fracture.
The untreated as-cast baseline has uniform dislocation transfer, no secondary phases, and high toughness under moderate loading.
The proposed behavior applies under high strain rates and severe mechanical loading.
Low thermal activation restricts recovery and favors localized stress concentrations.
The exact identity and evolution of any grain-boundary secondary phases are uncertain and may depend on compositional inhomogeneity or processing history.
The mechanism is falsified if severe loading produces neither detectable grain-boundary phase instability nor a statistically distinguishable toughness loss relative to the control.
